flags.finding: [partially supported] In S064, an armed robber enters the convenience store and shoots Dante point-blank in the chest behind the counter ('A gunshot blasts out. DANTE flies back, his chest exploding. He stares ahead and slumps to the floor.'). Staging a firearm discharge and an explosive chest blood hit on set presents significant safety, insurance, and liability hazards requiring strict specialized protocols. Live ammunition is strictly prohibited from production sets, and blank discharge requires dedicated qualified supervision, sightline clearance, and crew PPE.

citations.title: Safety Bulletin #1
citations.excerpt: BLANKS CAN KILL. TREAT ALL FIREARMS AS THOUGH THEY ARE LOADED. "LIVE AMMUNITION" IS NEVER TO BE USED NOR BROUGHT ONTO ANY STUDIO LOT OR STAGE.

remedy.detail: Retain a licensed armorer/property master to oversee all firearm storage, loading, and handling on set in accordance with CSATF Safety Bulletin #1. Conduct a mandatory safety meeting before blank discharge, establish a clear line-of-fire safety zone with protective shields/PPE for adjacent crew, and engage a licensed pyrotechnician/special effects coordinator to rig the practical chest squib hit. Alternatively, capture the muzzle flash and chest hit via pneumatic non-pyrotechnic rigs or post-production visual effects (VFX). Labor and permit costs range from $2,500 to $6,500, varying by shooting region and union agreements.

flags.finding: [partially supported] In S040, an ensemble hockey game is staged on the open roof of a commercial convenience store, featuring fast-paced athletic skating, body checks, stick battles ('Faces are smashed with sticks, slide tackles are made, shots are taken... Dante scrambles to the edge'), and a customer rapidly climbing an exterior ladder. Staging athletic stunts and rapid movement on an elevated, unprotected rooftop introduces severe fall and impact hazards governed by OSHA fall protection standards and stunt rigging safety regulations.

citations.title: 1926.501 - Duty to have fall protection. | Occupational Safety and Health Administration
citations.excerpt: each employee engaged in roofing activities on low-slope roofs, with unprotected sides and edges 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above lower levels shall be protected from falling by guardrail systems, safety net systems, personal fall arrest systems

citations.title: INDUSTRY WIDE LABOR-MANAGEMENT SAFETY COMMITTEE SAFETY BULLETIN #4 STUNTS
citations.excerpt: All equipment used for rigging must be inspected to check for wear, damage, and integrity prior to use. The Stunt Coordinator should approve the use of all rigging equipment. Any equipment found to be defective shall be removed from service. Fall protection may be required when rigging at heights.

remedy.detail: Engage a certified Stunt Coordinator and key rigging specialist to design a comprehensive rooftop fall-protection plan per OSHA 29 CFR 1926.501 and CSATF Safety Bulletin #4. Mandate temporary perimeter guardrails, safety netting, or low-profile personal fall-arrest harnesses with wire lines (to be removed digitally in post-production) for all performers within 15 feet of the roof edge. Install ground-level catch mats/crash pads below active shooting zones and secure all ladder access points. Labor, rigging, and equipment costs range from $5,000 to $15,000, varying by shooting region and union agreements.

flags.finding: In S031, Randal turns on the television in RST Video, and the script directs that 'The theme to Star Wars plays' as audio playback. Synchronizing the iconic musical composition 'Star Wars (Main Theme)' composed by John Williams with moving images requires a synchronization license from the copyright owners of the composition (Bantha Music / Warner-Tamerlane Publishing Corp. / Walt Disney Music). Major franchise themes carry substantial commercial sync fees that may be cost-prohibitive for independent productions. Split details should be confirmed via Songview prior to negotiations.

flags.finding: In S033, Dante physically wrestles with a Pringles potato chip canister painfully jammed on a customer's fist, while the customer argues the cans should carry government health warnings like cigarettes and expresses relief he avoided hospitalization. Depicting a branded consumer product (Pringles, owned by Kellanova / WK Kellogg Co) as physically hazardous and defective creates risk of trademark disparagement and trade libel claims during E&O insurance review. While satirical depiction in expressive works is often defensible, corporate brand owners actively police injurious packaging depictions.

citations.excerpt: A trademark is tarnished when it is used in such a way that consumers form an unfavorable or negative association with the mark, resulting in injury to the trademark holder’s business and reputation.

remedy.detail: Replace the branded Pringles container with a fictionalized, generic potato crisp cylindrical canister created by props (e.g., 'Crispy Stax'), or apply a custom label over the trade dress (fixed art department prop cost, approx. $50-$500). If retaining the dialogue reference, review with legal counsel to confirm expressive-use defense under script clearance guidelines.

flags.finding: [partially supported] In S009 and S010, the screenplay features a prominent Asbury Park Press newspaper rack and coin-operated vending machine outside the store, from which Dante extracts a full stack of newspapers after retrieving his coin. citations.title: Using Trademarks in Film and TV
citations.excerpt: Corporations live and die by their trademarks. A filmmaker has every right to dress sets with real products, but no right to disparage a trademark. If the movie does not misrepresent the source of the product there is typically no prohibition of the use of a trademark in a film.

remedy.detail: Obtain a publication and property release from Gannett / Asbury Park Press licensing department, or replace the vending machine graphics and newspaper masthead with a fictionalized regional periodical created by the art department (fixed art department prop cost, approx. $0-$500).

flags.finding: [partially supported] In S037, a customer holds and directly inspects the VHS home-video box packaging for 'Smokey and the Bandit Part 3' (Universal Pictures) during dialogue with Randal. citations.title: How does fair use work for book covers, album covers, and movie posters? - Ask A Librarian
citations.excerpt: Book covers, album covers, and movie covers are copyrightable. However, fair use, a provision of U.S. copyright law, gives users the right to use copyrighted material without permission under certain circumstances.

citations.excerpt: Getting clearance to use artwork in a movie or other filmed story is essential in an already collaborative process. An artwork release form allows a filmmaker to use a specific work of art or reproductions of that art while protecting the owner's rights.

remedy.detail: Have the art department fabricate a generic or parody home-video sleeve, or source a pre-cleared stock video prop from a motion picture clearance prop house (fixed prop cost, approx. $50-$500). flags.finding: [partially supported] In Scene S018, Jay references the Visa trademark in dialogue when dealing illicit drugs ('We take cash, or stolen MasterCard and Visa'). Associating a registered commercial trademark with criminal theft and illicit narcotics transactions creates product disparagement and trademark tarnishment exposure. While the dialogue use is likely defensible in an expressive work, brand owners actively protect marks against negative associations with criminal enterprise, potentially triggering E&O clearance objections or cease-and-desist demands.

citations.title: Using Trademarks in Film and TV
citations.excerpt: However, even if you have the right to use a trademark, you do not have the right to commit trade libel in the name of entertainment. Trade libel occurs when a product or service is falsely accused of some bad attribute.

remedy.detail: Replace the specific brand name 'Visa' in dialogue with a generic term such as 'credit cards' or a fictional card name. Modifying the spoken line incurs zero production cost and avoids trademark tarnishment inquiries.
